big: A client asks you for one thing: promise me at least 12% a year. It is easy to say yes and keep the client. It is also against the rules, and it can ruin the very person you are trying to help.

lines: Can you promise me at least 12% a year?
I cannot, and neither can anyone honest. Watch what a smooth 12% looks like against what a real market path looks like.

alt: A smooth 12 percent line against a bumpy made-up equity path
caps: A smooth 12% a year turns ₹100 into about ₹311 in ten years. This is the blue line.
The yellow line is a made-up equity path with ups and downs. These paths are made up.
Years 2, 5 and 8 fall. The deepest drop is about 18%.
It ends near ₹232, about 8.8% a year. No honest adviser can promise the blue line.
Build a plan that works even if returns are lower, and review it every year.

title: Say it, or never say it
stops: Market risks: read all scheme documents
Past performance may not be sustained
h: Say it, or never say it
alt: A shield with what must be said in mutual fund advertising and what must never be said
caps: Every mutual fund advertisement carries the standard risk statement.
Past performance can be shown only within the rules, with the line that it may not be sustained.
Never promise or imply a return, guarantee capital, or call a market-linked scheme safe.

q: A client says: I will invest if you promise 12% a year. What is the honest reply?
opts: I cannot promise it, but let us plan so that it works if returns are lower
I can promise it if you hold for at least ten years, as history shows
I can promise 12% only on diversified funds, not on single ones
I cannot say it aloud, but you can read it in the fund's brochure
why: No honest adviser can promise returns. A plan that survives lower returns, reviewed every year, is the fair answer.
History does not guarantee the future. A long holding period helps the odds, but it never makes a promise valid.
Diversified funds can fall as well. No type of fund carries a guaranteed return, so this promise is also false.
Brochures cannot promise returns either. Implying a return through any route is not allowed under the rules.

opts: Telling a client plainly that the fund's value can fall as well as rise
Showing a fund's five-year return along with the past performance line
Pushing a fund for its higher commission when a cheaper one fits better
Recording the client's goal, horizon and risk comfort before advising
why: Saying a fund can fall is an honest warning. It is the opposite of mis-selling, because it shows the risk.
Past performance may be shown within the rules and with the line that it may or may not be sustained.
Pushing a product for commission instead of the client's need is mis-selling. Suitability must come first.
Recording the goal, horizon and risk comfort is suitability. It is what the rules ask an adviser to do.

q: An advertisement says, 'Our fund gave 25% last year!' and nothing else. What is missing?
opts: The fund manager's name and photo beside the figure shown
Nothing, since a one-year figure is always allowed on its own
A guarantee that the 25% will be repeated again next year
The past performance line, and the standard market risk statement
why: A name or photo is not what the rules ask for. The risk statement and the past performance line are the missing parts.
A bare figure without the required lines is not allowed. The rules attach a disclaimer to past performance.
A guarantee would itself break the rules. Returns cannot be promised or implied, so a repeat cannot be assured.
Past performance may be shown only with the line that it may or may not be sustained, plus the standard risk statement.

q: Meena, 60 and retired, needs her money in two years. She asks for the best small cap fund because her neighbour made 40%. What does suitability say you do first?
opts: Place the order at once, since she is the client who asked for it
Record her goal, horizon and risk comfort, then judge if it fits
Choose the small cap fund that pays the adviser the highest commission
Tell her the 40% will repeat if she holds on for the two years
why: Just placing the order skips suitability. The adviser must check her goal, horizon and comfort with risk first.
Suitability comes first. A two-year goal for a retired client is a poor fit for a small cap fund, and the record shows why.
Choosing by commission is mis-selling. The client's need, not the adviser's pay, decides the recommendation.
No return can be guaranteed, and a neighbour's 40% says nothing about the next two years. Saying so breaks the rules.

pts: Never promise or imply a return, guarantee capital or call a scheme safe.
Always carry the market risk statement, and the past performance line when showing past returns.
Suitability before sale: record the goal, horizon and risk comfort.
